item.title: [8] Learning the limits of protein structure models with NMR chemical shifts
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

Wayment-Steele's lab benchmarks protein foundation models against NMR chemical shifts and finds the largest errors in core residues with fast dynamics, which is a direct critique of what structure models learn about dynamics and ties to experimental-data validation of your ensemble work.

Zhao, C., El Nesr, G., Chen, Y., Wayment-Steele, H. K.

Protein foundation models are intended to implicitly learn the chemical rules underlying protein function. However, systematically evaluating what biochemistry these models have learned remains difficult, as most downstream tasks lack experimental data fine-grained enough to expose their failure modes. NMR chemical shifts fill this gap: as direct per-atom reporters of local chemical environment, they offer a sensitive probe of structure-based representations. In this work, we present a systematically curated chemical shift dataset designed to minimize experimental confounders. We use it to benchmark diverse protein foundation models in their ability to predict backbone 15N chemical shifts, atoms that are known to be sensitive to many effects. The largest error across all models is in core residues with evidence of fast-timescale dynamics, which we investigate mechanistically using molecular dynamics simulations. Given the biological relevance of structured dynamic regions, we trained a new model based on the best of these embeddings, SLAE, to predict its own error. SLAE-ERR achieves a mean absolute error of 0.76 ppm for predicting error. Together, we hope that the datasets, evaluation tasks, and models presented here are sources of guidance for protein design model improvement.

item.title: [7] Manifold Attracting Flow Matching: Physics-Constrained Sampling via Continuous Geometric Dynamics
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Manifold Attracting Flow Matching replaces repeated endpoint corrections with a continuous ODE that contracts constraint violations while preserving model-guided motion, a genuinely new take on inference-time constraint steering that could transfer to enforcing experimental restraints.

Guanyu Chen, Jinchen Wang, Shengze Xu, Xingyu Ren, Tieyong Zeng, Antonios Armaou, Dong Ni

arXiv:2611.16677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generating scientific data under previously unseen equality constraints requires satisfying the prescribed constraints without destroying the physical structure learned from data. Existing inference-time approaches often enforce physical constraints by repeatedly correcting predicted endpoints, but such discrete corrections can distort learned generative structure and introduce unstable feedback. In this work, we propose Manifold Attracting Flow Matching (MAFM), which continuously evolves a persistent anchor through an ODE whose dynamics drive it analytically toward the constraint manifold. Specifically, its geometric correction preserves model-guided tangent motion while prescribing the normal motion to contract constraint violations toward the manifold. This construction separates model tracking from constraint attraction and provides theoretical guarantees for residual contraction and local feedback stabilization. Experiments across geometric and partial differential equation benchmarks demonstrate improved generation quality over variant constraint-guided baselines while maintaining low constraint residuals. MAFM provides a flexible framework for coordinating learned physical structure and explicit constraints through controllable sampling dynamics, without retraining the underlying generative model.

item.title: [8] PolyFold: Homology Filtering Approach Alters Apparent Structure Prediction Model Performances
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

A head-to-head Boltz-2 vs OpenFold 3 benchmark showing that conventional minimum-chain homology filtering leaves training-data leakage in multichain complexes and inflates apparent performance, which bears directly on how you evaluate the cofolding models sampleworks steers.

Stephenson, H., Voicu, D., Novakov, V., Levy, M. et al.

As structure prediction models become increasingly central to biological research and drug discovery, rigorous and reproducible benchmarking is critical to assess model performance and generalization. PolyFold is an end-to-end workflow automation and benchmarking framework that streamlines input file creation, batch automation, and a more conservative evaluation of model performances. We conduct a head-to-head comparison of Boltz-2 and OpenFold 3 - leading open-source alternatives to AlphaFold 3. We first curate an evaluation set of several thousand high-quality PDB structures, homology-filtered against both models' training sets, then automate inference and evaluation using PolyFold. Using a cluster analysis, we directly connect features of the underlying structures to model performance profiles, demonstrating the nonrandom nature of failure and success modes. While initial analyses using conventional homology filtering techniques show performance differences favouring Boltz-2, we show that using minimum chain fractional identity for novelty filtering can cause residual training-data leakage in multichain complexes, inflating apparent performances. To address this, we introduce a length-weighted average fractional identity (WAFI) for whole-complex homology filtering. This provides a more conservative evaluation by reducing residual leakage. While Boltz-2 maintains higher aggregate metric averages for categories such as nucleic acid-containing structures, membrane-bound proteins, and antibody-antigen complexes, the performance gap significantly narrows or disappears for effectively all partitions after implementing WAFI filtering, demonstrating the need for more stringent conventions in homology filtering. Both models still struggle with homomultimers, small molecule realism, and structures with non-canonical amino acids, demonstrating persisting limitations in the field. In summary, PolyFold enables practitioners to rapidly compare models on a variety of inference tasks and supports the broader adoption of accessible computational tools to facilitate biomolecular science.

item.title: [8] REVEAL: RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

It shows that AF3, Boltz-2, OpenFold3, and Protenix-v2 all place HIV-1 TAR near the ground state and invert the NMR-observed population ordering, a direct failure analysis of cofolding models for conformational ensembles that motivates experimentally steered sampling.

Bhakat, S., Vats, S.

Capturing the sparsely populated but functionally important, excited states of RNA remains a central challenge for molecular simulation, because the underlying transitions are rare events that unbiased molecular dynamics cannot reach from a single starting structure. Here we introduce REVEAL (RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes), a workflow that couples generative secondary structure sampling, secondary structure conditioned tertiary structure prediction with trRosettaRNA2, unbiased molecular dynamics and Markov state modeling. Using only the sequence of the engineered HIV-1 TAR mutant, in which the excited state ES2 is the dominant conformation, we show that REVEAL captures the reversible ES2 to GS register shift from 6.8 s of aggregate unbiased sampling across 34 seeds, recovering both basins, the intermediate states, and correctly identifies ES2 as the dominant state, consistent with the design of the construct. In contrast, molecular dynamics seeded from the ES2-dominant HIV-1 TAR mutant NMR ensemble remains trapped in ES2 despite substantially longer aggregate simulation time, and sequence-only ensemble predictors (AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, ESMFold2, OpenFold3 and Protenix-v2) place every structure near the ground state and invert the experimentally observed population ordering. The information content of the seed ensemble, rather than the total simulation time, determines whether the transition is sampled. We further introduce ''population-weighted consensus score'' (PWCS) that ranks conformers by how representative they are of the equilibrium ensemble directly from the simulation data, without experimental restraints and independent of the choice of collective variables. PWCS identifies the dominant state even when low-dimensional representations fail to separate the states. Built entirely from open-source tools, REVEAL provides a transparent and extensible route to RNA conformational ensembles beyond the single-structure paradigm.

item.title: [8] Leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors to generate atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

Bonomi's bAIes now builds atomistic IDP ensembles from the distance distributions of AlphaFold3, Boltz-1, and Boltz-2 and validates them against NMR and SAXS, directly bridging cofolding-model outputs and experimental-data-driven ensemble generation as in your work.

Schnapka, V., Portal, N., Bonomi, M.

Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are central to many biological processes, but their function depends on dynamic conformational ensembles rather than a single structure. Despite the impact of artificial intelligence on protein structure prediction, determining these ensembles at atomistic resolution remains challenging. Recently, we introduced bAIes, a framework that leverages the structural information encoded in AlphaFold2 distograms to generate conformational ensembles of IDPs at atomistic resolution. Here, we extend this framework to six state-of-the-art structure prediction tools (AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3, Boltz-1, Boltz-2, ESMFold, and ESMFold2) and systematically compare the structural information encoded in their predicted inter-residue distance distributions. Despite differences between predictors, we show that bAIes generates ensembles with comparable accuracy against experimental NMR and SAXS data, and competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art all-atom simulations and alternative IDP ensemble generation methods. These results demonstrate that bAIes is robust to the choice of structure predictor and that the distance distributions generated by different deep learning architectures contain valuable information about the conformational preferences of disordered proteins. More broadly, our work highlights the potential of combining AI-derived structural information with physics-based modeling to generate atomistic ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins and regions.

item.title: [7] An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

A tutorial by Dai and Du unifying diffusion, flows, variational inference, score matching and inference-time composition under energy-based models is the kind of long expository piece that supports guidance and composition ideas in your work.

Bo Dai, Yilun Du

arXiv:2611.14383v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_\theta(x)\propto\exp(-E_\theta(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.

item.title: [7] AdjointFlow: Accelerating Scientific Inverse Problems with Physics-Based Transport
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

AdjointFlow injects the known forward physics into stochastic-interpolant transport to solve inverse problems far faster than plug-and-play methods, which is directly analogous to using a differentiable forward model (structure factors or map calculation) with a flow prior.

Ethan Hanold, Nicholas M. Boffi, Qin Li, Leonardo Zepeda-N\'u\~nez

arXiv:2611.13389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inverse problems are ubiquitous across scientific applications ranging from seismic imaging to astrophysics to nondestructive testing, yet classical solvers often struggle with nonconvexity and repeated evaluations of expensive physical models. Diffusion models can amortize this computation offline, but largely data-driven conditional models underutilize known physics and suffer from ill-conditioned transport maps when the target distribution is concentrated. Plug-and-play (PnP) methods explicitly leverage the physical model to guide a learned prior, improving data consistency but reintroducing costly iterative computations. We instead propose AdjointFlow, a framework built on stochastic interpolants that injects the known physics into the generative transport itself. We design a data-dependent, adjoint-based initialization to reduce transport distance to the target, modify the transport velocity to remain regular as the endpoint distributions concentrate, and parameterize the network to build the initialization directly into the learned velocity. Together, these enable accurate reconstruction at substantially lower cost than generative models starting from Gaussian noise. Experiments on inverse scattering, seismic imaging, and black hole imaging show that AdjointFlow consistently produces more accurate reconstructions than conditional diffusion models while being up to five orders of magnitude faster at inference than PnP methods. Optional inference-time refinement that queries the physical model can further improve data consistency, matching or exceeding the accuracy of PnP methods without retraining.

item.title: [7] Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Pyrite benchmarks ranking of candidate poses generated by cofolding models, showing expert chemists near chance and LLM agents beating them, which is a direct evaluation-methodology and agent-for-structure result relevant to judging cofolding outputs.

Megha Srivastava, Michael H. Lim, Allison M. Keys, Pranav Murugan, Nate Gruver

arXiv:2611.14511v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.

item.title: [7] Membrane Geometry Reveals Strengths and Limitations of AlphaFold-Predicted Transmembrane Protein Complexes
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

This paper systematically evaluates AlphaFold-Multimer and AF3 on transmembrane complexes, showing high-confidence predictions can be geometrically implausible and that AF3 struggles with cholesterol-binding poses past its training cutoff, which is the kind of cofolding failure analysis and evaluation methodology you track.

Sziklai, D., Wiener, Z., Padanyi, R., Hegedus, T.

High-confidence protein complex predictions do not necessarily represent physically or biologically plausible assemblies. This limitation is particularly relevant for transmembrane (TM) proteins, whose interactions are constrained by the lipid bilayer. Here, we systematically evaluated membrane compatibility in the recently expanded AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, analysing 189,469 high-confidence AlphaFold-Multimer TM-TM complexes and additional TM-soluble assemblies. Most predictions exhibited plausible membrane geometry: among 125,657 evaluable complexes with TM proteins possessing more than two TM helices, 95.4% had joint hydrophobic thicknesses within the expected range of 15-35 angstroms. Nevertheless, some complexes displayed substantial inconsistencies in membrane positioning or protomer orientation despite favourable prediction confidence. Interactions between TM proteins, particularly those containing only one or two TM helices, were frequently dominated by extramembrane contacts. Among TM-soluble complexes, 77.4% showed no penetration of the soluble partner into the hydrophobic membrane core. We further investigated whether AlphaFold3 (AF3) could overcome limitations of AlphaFold-Multimer. Although AF3 recovered an experimentally supported SERCA-phospholamban interaction, it failed to reproduce the cholesterol-mediated norepinephrine transporter homodimer. A benchmark of 173 cholesterol-containing membrane protein targets further revealed limited accuracy in predicting cholesterol-binding poses, particularly for structures released after the AF3 training cutoff. Together, these findings demonstrate that membrane-specific geometric constraints provide a valuable complement to conventional confidence metrics and highlight the persistent challenges of predicting assemblies involving lipids.

item.title: [10] Co-folding model guided by structural proteomics
item.description:
Score 10/10 · arXiv

AIMS-Fold is inference-time guidance on Boltz-2 using structural-proteomics restraints, including repulsive ones, lifting failing PROTAC and glue complexes from 14% to 86% success, which is almost exactly the experimental-data steering of cofolding models you build.

Alon Shtrikman, Sagie Brodsky, Michal Ran Shchory, Nitzan Simchi, Yaron Ben Shoshan-Galeczki, Eran Seger, Kirill Pevzner

arXiv:2605.26192v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Proximity-inducing drugs, including PROTACs, represent a promising therapeutic modality. Their activity is driven by the geometry of the assembled ternary complex, which determines whether the target is ubiquitinated. Co-folding models perform poorly in these cases due to scarcity of training data and the dynamic nature of such complexes. Structural proteomics can supply the missing geometric information and steer the model towards an accurate prediction. However, current models accept only positive signals, while a differential structural mass-spectrometry experiment also reports negative signals. We introduce AIMS-Fold, an inference-time guidance layer built on Boltz-2 that requires no retraining and accepts repulsive constraints alongside attractive ones. We tested AIMS-Fold on 28 PROTAC, glue and antibody complexes that Boltz-2 fails to predict. From only five generated models, guidance recovers the correct conformation in 64% of cases. The gap does not close with scale: across 100 models and 20 seeds, unguided Boltz-2 reaches 14% while AIMS-Fold reaches 86%. Repulsive constraints alone recover the correct conformation on some systems, occasionally exceeding the matched attractive constraints. Taken together, these results demonstrate the strength of utilizing the full structural proteomics signal, positive and negative, to steer generative models toward the correct conformation, addressing a central problem in rational degrader design.

item.title: [8] Test-time scaling of diffusions with flow maps
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Flow Map Trajectory Tilting from Vanden-Eijnden, Albergo and Boffi gives a provably better reward-gradient steering of diffusion via flow maps, with exact importance-weighted sampling, directly relevant to inference-time steering of generative models with measurement-like rewards.

Amirmojtaba Sabour, Michael S. Albergo, Carles Domingo-Enrich, Nicholas M. Boffi, Sanja Fidler, Karsten Kreis, Eric Vanden-Eijnden

arXiv:2511.22688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A common recipe to improve diffusion models at test-time so that samples score highly against a user-specified reward is to introduce the gradient of the reward into the dynamics of the diffusion itself. This procedure is often ill posed, as user-specified rewards are usually only well defined on the data distribution at the end of generation. While common workarounds to this problem are to use a denoiser to estimate what a sample would have been at the end of generation, we propose a simple solution to this problem by working directly with a flow map. By exploiting a relationship between the flow map and velocity field governing the instantaneous transport, we construct an algorithm, Flow Map Trajectory Tilting (FMTT), which provably performs better ascent on the reward than standard test-time methods involving the gradient of the reward. The approach can be used to either perform exact sampling via importance weighting or principled search that identifies local maximizers of the reward-tilted distribution. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach against other look-ahead techniques, and show how the flow map enables engagement with complicated reward functions that make possible new forms of image editing, e.g. by interfacing with vision language models.

item.title: [8] Geometry and Stochastic Analysis of Flow and Diffusion Models: A Survey
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

A survey unifying flow and diffusion models through geometry, Wiener-space integration by parts, conditioning, Schrödinger bridges, and manifold and function-space extensions is a long expository piece directly on the mathematics behind your guidance work.

Ehsan Mirafzali, Razvan Marinescu

arXiv:2611.12107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flow-based and diffusion-based models have become the principal means of learning and sampling high-dimensional probability distributions, from images and video to proteins, molecules and physical fields, and increasingly language. Each carries a simple law to the law of the data along a curve of probability measures, and behind the variety of their names lie three geometries, those of the state space on which the data live, of the space of probability measures through which the curve passes, and of the space of paths traced by the generating process. A single analytic idea runs through the subject. Every score identity used to train a diffusion model is an integration by parts, on the noise, on the data or on Wiener space, and Malliavin calculus extends this to nonlinear and infinite-dimensional diffusions. We develop these foundations with full definitions and follow them through normalising flows, flow matching and few-step maps, diffusion models and their convergence theory, conditioning, Schr\"odinger bridges and stochastic control, and their extension to manifolds, Lie groups, discrete and function spaces and jump processes. We close with statistical physics, renormalisation and, more speculatively, holography, in which the radial direction of anti-de Sitter space can play the role of flow time. A table of the main methods and a collection of open problems complete the survey.

item.title: [8] An Introduction to Applied Probability and Stochastic Processes: Open Lecture Notes
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Open lecture notes on measure-theoretic probability, SDEs, stochastic calculus and Monte Carlo with exercises and solutions are exactly the kind of foundational exposition underpinning diffusion and SMC methods you want flagged.

Matthew Lorig

arXiv:2611.10948v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: These open lecture notes provide a broad introduction to measure-theoretic probability and stochastic processes, with a focus on applications. Topics include probability spaces, conditional expectation, generating and characteristic functions, Markov chains in discrete and continuous time, convergence of random variables, Brownian motion, stochastic calculus, stochastic differential equations and their connection to partial differential equations, jump diffusions, stochastic control, optimal stopping, and Monte Carlo methods. Most chapters include exercises, and solutions are provided. The notes were written for a two-quarter course for first-year PhD students in applied mathematics, and should also be useful to graduate students in statistics, engineering, economics and finance. The LaTeX source is freely available on GitHub under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license, and readers are encouraged to fork the notes and contribute corrections, improvements, and new material.

item.title: [8] OriDynamics: Towards a World Model for Biomolecular Dynamics
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

OriDynamics generates all-atom ensembles for monomers and complexes with ensemble-level supervision on fluctuations and covariance, a direct BioEmu-style competitor you should benchmark against.

Jiahao Yang, Dong Liu, Hongliang Li, Ji Chen, Yuehua Liu, Daoyun Ding, Duo An, Jun Li, Jiahua Rao, Ziqiao Zhang, Peicong Lin, Shuangjia Zheng

arXiv:2611.11958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biomolecular recognition and regulation depend on atomic interactions that change as molecular partners fluctuate and adopt alternative conformations. Modeling these processes requires ensembles that capture both conformational diversity and coordinated atomic fluctuations between interacting molecules. Here we present OriDynamics, a unified framework for all-atom ensemble generation across protein monomers and complexes with small molecules or protein partners. OriDynamics introduces a latent ensemble decomposition that couples broad conformational exploration in a compact structural latent space with local all-atom sampling around generated proposals. Ensemble-level supervision constrains mean positions, fluctuation amplitudes and joint coordinate covariance to capture coordinated atomic variability within and between molecular partners. Across benchmarks of proteins and their complexes, OriDynamics demonstrates superior overall performance in conformational coverage, atomic fluctuation fidelity and interaction geometry compared with leading baselines. Application studies further demonstrate recovery of alternative functional conformations and partner-dependent changes in conformational ensembles alongside sampling of configurations associated with ligand dissociation. These capabilities provide a foundation for a biomolecular world model that represents accessible molecular states and their dependence on interaction context.

item.title: [8] Realism and resolution: How AI-predicted protein structures differ from experimental structures
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

WhatRes quantifies how AI-predicted structures are over-idealised in bond geometry relative to experimental structures, which is directly relevant to evaluating cofolding outputs and to validation metrics when using them as priors for refinement.

van der Kant, R., Delgado Blanco, J., Serrano, L., Schymkowitz, J. et al.

Protein structure predictors can recover protein folds with remarkable accuracy, and their models are increasingly used as if they were experimental structures. Yet even for a confidently predicted fold, it remains difficult to judge how faithfully the model reproduces protein geometry. We introduce WhatRes, which assesses a structure from its coordinates on two complementary axes. Apparent resolution estimates the experimental resolution its local geometry most closely resembles. Realism measures how closely that geometry matches experimental structures at the same apparent resolution. Predicted models can score well on apparent resolution while showing systematically less variation in bond lengths and angles than is observed in high-resolution crystal structures. WhatRes reveals this over-idealisation even in high-confidence models.

item.title: [7] Stitched Value Model for Diffusion Alignment
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

StitchVM learns amortized value functions on noisy latents to improve FK steering and accelerate DPS, directly targeting the cost and bias of Tweedie-style guidance you rely on, though it is demonstrated on images rather than molecules.

Hyojun Go, Hyungjin Chung, Prune Truong, Goutam Bhat, Li Mi, Zhaochong An, Zixiang Zhao, Dominik Narnhofer, Serge Belongie, Federico Tombari, Konrad Schindler

arXiv:2605.19804v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reward-based alignment of diffusion and flow models requires estimating the value function at noisy intermediate latents, although pretrained reward models operate on clean images. Common approaches use Tweedie-style clean-image proxies or Monte Carlo rollouts, introducing approximation bias or substantial computational cost. Directly learning the value function offers an alternative, but matching the performance and generalization of foundation-scale pixel-space reward models on noisy latents remains challenging. We address this gap by transferring pretrained reward capabilities to noisy latents. We propose \textbf{StitchVM} (Stitched Value Model), a model stitching framework that connects a frozen diffusion-backbone prefix to a pretrained reward-model suffix through a compatible feature interface. A closed-form feature fit selects the interface, and lightweight distillation adapts the stitched model, combining noise-aware diffusion features with pretrained reward capability. For example, adapting CLIP ViT-L with SD~3.5 Medium at $512\times512$ resolution takes approximately 10 GPU-hours on a single GH200. Once trained, StitchVM provides an amortized alternative to Tweedie-style and Monte Carlo approximations of the value function: it estimates value directly from noisy latents, avoiding clean-image reconstruction and additional denoising rollouts for each evaluation. We demonstrate benefits across inference-time steering and post-training. StitchVM improves the quality and efficiency of FK steering and DRaFT, accelerates DPS by $3.7\times$ with half the peak GPU memory, and accelerates DiffusionNFT by $2.3\times$.

item.title: [7] Learnable Chernoff Baselines for Inference-Time Alignment
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Learnable Chernoff Baselines give a black-box, rejection-sampling route to reward-tilted sampling from pretrained continuous and discrete diffusion models with TV guarantees, which is a fairly new inference-time steering idea that could transfer to data-guided sampling in Boltz-style models, though it is not demonstrated on structure.

Sunil Madhow, Yuchen Liang, Ness Shroff, Yingbin Liang, Yu-Xiang Wang

arXiv:2602.07738v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study inference-time reward-guided alignment for generative models. Existing methods often rely on either architecture-specific adaptations or computationally costly inference procedures. We introduce Learnable Chernoff Baselines (LCBs) as a method for efficiently and approximately sampling from the exponentially tilted kernels that arise from KL-regularized reward alignment. Using only black-box sampling access to the pretrained model, LCBs implement a form of rejection sampling with adaptively selected acceptance probabilities, which allows fine-grained control over inference-compute scaling. We establish total-variation guarantees to the ideal aligned model, and demonstrate in both continuous and discrete diffusion settings that LCB sampling closely matches ideal rejection sampling while using substantially fewer queries to the pretrained model.

item.title: [7] Spectral Feedback for Test-Time Alignment of Protein Diffusion Models
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Test-time alignment of discrete diffusion for protein inverse folding via learned re-masking and re-sampling of edit positions is a new steering idea in a protein generative model, though it is sequence-level with a stability oracle rather than experimental data.

Shai Dickman, Mert Cemri, Landon Butler, Kannan Ramchandran

arXiv:2609.30456v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discrete diffusion models have become leading architectures for inverse protein folding. Test-time alignment guides these models during inference to generate proteins with desirable attributes. Alignment methods for discrete diffusion models often treat inference as a unidirectional process, lacking effective mechanisms for revisiting undesirable token selections. We introduce Spectral Feedback, an algorithm that selects edit-positions in a feedback loop, allowing the model to iteratively correct its own generations. This approach leverages the masking structure of discrete diffusion models by re-masking and re-sampling tokens. While prior alignment methods focus on what token labels to assign to maximize a target reward, we instead treat which tokens to revisit as the central alignment problem. Selecting edit-positions is challenging because edit effects are interdependent: the impact of modifying one token depends on which others are edited simultaneously. We define an edit-set as a set of positions to edit by re-masking and re-sampling the corresponding tokens in a sequence. Motivated by prior work on sparse interactions in biological systems, we find empirically that edit-set value functions for protein inverse folding admit sparse Fourier representations. This structure enables Spectral Feedback to efficiently learn and optimize the value functions for edit-position selection. Spectral Feedback is model-agnostic and can be applied to pre-trained, test-time aligned, and fine-tuned diffusion models without modifying the underlying generative processes. Applied to inverse folding with a protein stability reward oracle, Spectral Feedback increases the proportion of stable proteins by 32.3 percentage points over a pre-trained model, 24.8 over Best-of-10, and 5.8 over a state-of-the-art RL fine-tuned diffusion model.

item.title: [7] Multilevel and Sequential Monte Carlo for Training-Free Diffusion Guidance
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

An unbiased SMC estimator with multilevel Monte Carlo variance reduction for training-free diffusion guidance directly attacks the point-estimate bias in DPS-style posterior approximation that steering methods rely on.

Aidan Gleich, Scott C. Schmidler

arXiv:2601.21104v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We address the problem of accurate, training-free guidance for conditional generation in trained diffusion models. Existing methods typically rely on point-estimates to approximate the posterior score, often resulting in biased approximations that fail to capture multimodality inherent to the reverse process of diffusion models. We propose a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) framework that integrates over the full denoising distribution to construct an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of $p_\theta(y\mid x_t)$, avoiding the bias of existing training-free guidance methods. To ensure computational tractability, we incorporate variance-reduction schemes based on MultiLevel Monte Carlo (MLMC). We evaluate on three image generation tasks. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classifier guidance, our approach improves accuracy by 18 and 38 points respectively over the strongest training-free baseline. On CelebA-HQ joint-attribute guidance, three existing methods (DPS, LGD, TFG) used within our framework all outperform the closest SMC-based comparator (TDS) by 25-37 points, and improve over the strongest baseline by 2-14 points.

item.title: [7] Efficient and Accurate Zero Shot Generation of Symmetric Protein Complexes
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

ZeUS turns pretrained SE(3)-equivariant backbone generators like RFdiffusion into symmetric assembly generators without retraining via a quotient-space argument, a transferable idea for constrained sampling in structure models.

Rory Gao, Yuanzhou Chen, Prajit Rajkumar, Wei Wang

arXiv:2611.10424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symmetric organization is a fundamental principle of biomolecular complex assembly. The same principle underlies engineered applications, from vaccine platforms to nanomaterials, making symmetric de novo generation a core capability for computational protein design. We establish a theoretical foundation equating generation of an assembly with underlying symmetry group $G$ to generation within a quotient space over $G$. This directly allows $\mathrm{SE}(3)$-equivariant models to generate symmetric structures with minimal distribution shift. With this insight we introduce ZeUS ($\textbf{Ze}$ro-shot $\textbf{U}$nified $\textbf{S}$ymmetrization), a framework that converts any pretrained $\mathrm{SE}(3)$-equivariant backbone generative model into an efficient generator of symmetric assemblies with no retraining. ZeUS operates on a single $\textit{canonical subunit}$ and utilizes $\textit{phantom subunits}$ to preserve internal model operations, reducing memory and runtime cost by $\mathcal{O}(|G|)$ for finite groups $G$, compared to a full-complex forward pass. We implement ZeUS for IPA-based models (FrameDiff, FoldFlow) and axial-attention-based RFdiffusion, showing high generation efficiency with minimal degradation to generation quality. We then apply ZeUS to generate symmetric complexes of over $10{,}000$ residues with exact, untruncated attention, a scale previously intractable with any model.

item.title: [7] Rapid generation of antibody conformational ensembles using machine learning
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Cadense is an ML generator of antibody Fv conformational ensembles trained on MD that recovers apo and holo states, squarely in your ensemble-emulator (BioEmu-style) interest, though it is antibody-specific and not steered by experimental data.

Rao, P. V., Sommer, D., Davidson, D., Alberstein, R. G. et al.

We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody antigen interactions. Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.

item.title: [8] Diffusion-free Score Matching for Exact Conditional Sampling
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

DISCO enables exact conditional sampling from score-based models without time-dependent scores, directly addressing the conditioning-on-observations problem that underlies steering generative models with experimental data.

Thomas Wedenig, Robert Peharz

arXiv:2611.09758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The success of modern score-based generative models is largely driven by diffusion-based training, which learns a collection of time-indexed score fields corresponding to progressively noisier versions of the data distribution. While such models achieve impressive sample quality, leveraging them for sound probabilistic inference---particularly sampling from arbitrary conditionals of the model---remains challenging. This difficulty arises because conditioning information is only available for clean data and not for the higher noise levels required to generate exact conditional samples. In this paper, we introduce DIffusion-free SCOre matching (DISCO), a principled approach that sidesteps the need for time-dependent score fields altogether. Our method is based on an objective that, while reminiscent of diffusion-based training, estimates only a single score of the (slightly perturbed) data distribution, for which the exact conditional score is readily obtained. In experiments, DISCO is competitive with state-of-the-art diffusion models in terms of sample quality. More importantly, DISCO yields a more faithful representation of the underlying data distribution and---crucially---enables accurate sampling from arbitrary conditionals, outperforming standard heuristic samplers. This capability opens the door to principled and flexible probabilistic reasoning with score-based models.

item.title: [8] Measuring and Decomposing Mode Separation via the Canonical Diffusion
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Quantifying mode separation and metastable directions from samples plus a score function via a canonical diffusion, with pretrained score models and alanine-dipeptide conformations as a test, offers a label-free way to assess conformational ensembles from generative models.

Shaul Tolkovsky, Ori Meidler, Or Zuk

arXiv:2605.08777v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mode separation, namely how sharply a distribution fragments into barrier-separated clusters, is a fundamental geometric property of densities, difficult to quantify in high dimensions. Modes are often the meaningful alternatives in the data, such as the conformations of a molecule or the distinct semantic types among a generative model's outputs. Mode separation is distinct from dispersion, which is what standard label-free tools capture: differential entropy rises with spread regardless of fragmentation, and PCA orders directions by variance regardless of barriers. Mutual information does capture it, but only given the latent component labels, which are usually unavailable. We measure mode separation through a single stochastic process intrinsic to the density, namely the unique reversible diffusion with $f$ as its stationary distribution and a constant scalar diffusion coefficient. From its autocovariance matrix we extract two readouts. The first, SSA (Sum of Squared Autocorrelations), is a scalar barrier-sensitive measure. The second, DA (Dominant Autocorrelation directions), gives linear projections ordered by metastability rather than variance. Under an isotropic-Gaussian null, we derive the limiting spectrum of the empirical autocovariance in closed form, generalizing the Marchenko--Pastur law. Its upper edge gives a noise floor that separates metastable directions from sampling noise. Both readouts use only samples and a score function, scaling to high dimensions through pretrained score-based generative models via Tweedie's identity. We apply our framework to three settings: (i) synthetic Gaussian mixtures, where SSA tracks mutual information; (ii) SDXL text-to-image generations, where SSA and DA capture structure that entropy and PCA miss; and (iii) molecular dynamics of alanine dipeptide, where DA recovers the known slow backbone dihedrals from static samples alone.

item.title: [8] CoMoFlow: Controllable Protein Conformational Ensemble Generation via Explicit Collective-Mode Modeling
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

CoMoFlow adds explicit collective-mode conditioning to SE(3) flow matching for controllable backbone ensembles on ATLAS, directly in your conformational-ensemble generation area, though it does not use experimental data.

Yusong Wang, Zheyuan Gu, Ailiang Lin, Minghao Shao, Yicheng Xu, Jiang Cai, Prayag Tiwari, Mingkun Xu

arXiv:2611.09548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein conformational ensemble generation aims to efficiently characterize the structural variations accessible to a protein beyond a single static structure. Recent flow-based methods efficiently generate conformational ensembles, but they model coordinated structural variation implicitly, which can limit ensemble fidelity and hinder direct control. To address this limitation, we propose CoMoFlow, a controllable framework for generating protein backbone conformational ensembles by explicitly modeling collective variation. CoMoFlow constructs protein-specific collective modes from the equilibrium structure, learns the distribution of their coefficients across the molecular dynamics (MD) ensemble, and uses sampled collective variations to guide SE(3) flow matching through feature conditioning and prior recentering. Experiments on ATLAS and de novo proteins show that CoMoFlow improves reconstruction of MD conformational distributions and coordinated structural variation relative to strong flow-based baselines, while enabling direct control over targeted conformational changes.

item.title: [7] Atomic Trajectory Modeling with State Space Models for Biomolecular Dynamics
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

ATMOS is a Pairformer-plus-diffusion state space model that autoregressively generates atomistic MD trajectories, which is close to BioEmu-style ensemble emulation, though it targets dynamics rather than experimental-data steering.

Liang Shi, Jiarui Lu, Junqi Liu, Chence Shi, Zhi Yang, Jian Tang

arXiv:2603.17633v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding the dynamic behavior of biomolecules is fundamental to elucidating biological function and facilitating drug discovery.While Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations provide a rigorous physical basis for studying these dynamics, they remain computationally expensive for long timescales.Recent deep generative models accelerate conformation generation but often either discard temporal correlations entirely or struggle to condition on the extended history required for faithful kinetics, a consequence of the effectively non-Markovian nature of partially observed subsystem coordinates.To bridge this gap, we introduce ATMOS, a novel generative framework based on State Space Models (SSM) designed to generate atom-level MD trajectories for biomolecular systems.ATMOS integrates a Pairformer-based state transition mechanism to capture temporal dependencies, with a diffusion-based module to decode trajectory frames autoregressively.We demonstrate that ATMOS achieves state-of-the-art performance in generating conformation trajectories for both protein monomers and protein-ligand systems.This work provides a unified and computationally efficient framework for biomolecular trajectory generation, taking a step toward dynamics foundation models.
